claims.text: Free-energy landscape mapping during reactive processing will reveal an optimal processing window for a controlled, large-scale reaction at the Cu–refractory interface.
The identified processing window will produce a uniform, stable microstructure despite the positive heat of mixing between Cu and refractory elements.
Conventional mixing of a refractory high-entropy alloy with copper typically produces an inhomogeneous microstructure because interdiffusion is limited.
Accelerated Monte Carlo or molecular-dynamics-based free-energy sampling can guide reactive-processing parameters.
Optimized high-temperature dwell times and cooling rates can promote a metastable reaction pathway at the Cu–refractory interface.
A metastable interfacial reaction zone enhances interdiffusion and bonding between the copper and refractory phases.
Free-energy mapping identifies processing windows that lower the effective thermodynamic barrier associated with positive heat of mixing.
Lowering the effective thermodynamic barrier permits controlled interfacial reactions.
Controlled interfacial reactions produce uniform interdiffusion and a stable microstructure.
The resulting microstructure can withstand high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
The proposed processing approach will improve microstructural homogeneity and interfacial bonding.
Improved homogeneity and interfacial bonding will yield better mechanical strength and irradiation resistance.
Conventional mixing and sintering produce multiphase, inhomogeneous Cu–refractory microstructures because of strong thermodynamic immiscibility.
The approach may fail when intrinsic free-energy barriers lie outside the accessible processing window or metastable states cannot be reproduced.
The required temperature, dwell time, and cooling rate are unknown and require empirical calibration.
